GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: Precipitation chances continue into Friday afternoon, though coverage will gradually taper off. Meanwhile, the low pressure system will be absorbed into the main flow, driving a frontal passage through the area.
GJT.text:
ISOLATED SHOWERS AND SEASONABLE TEMPS TO BEGIN THE WORK WEEK:

Broad southwesterly flow will dominate the start of the work week, maintaining moisture advection across the region. Expect increasing cloud cover along with isolated showers through Tuesday. Modest warm air advection will nudge high temperatures closer to seasonal normals despite the increased cloud cover. While localized breezy conditions could accompany collapsing showers, organized convection is not anticipated.

By Wednesday, a strong low pressure system drops southward along the California coast, while an upper level jet noses into the Four Corners region. These two features will work in tandem to bring remnant moisture from what is now Hurricane Trudy into the region, bringing the return of widespread precipitation chances. Initial model solutions depict the most likely time period for widespread showers to be Wednesday night through Thursday night. It is also important to note that a large majority of the precipitation from this system will fall as rain, with the pool of colder temperatures staying well north of the forecast area. As a result, snow levels will remain high, generally at or above 12,000 feet. Given the prospect of high-elevation rain falling onto antecedent snowpack and saturated soils from last week's precipitation, flash flooding and hydrologic impacts will be monitored closely as the system progresses. Ensemble guidance supports PWATs upwards of 250-300% of normal, providing another strong signal to monitor for potential impacts. Keep in mind that the forecast remains fluid this far out, and key details may shift over the coming days. Stay tuned for updates.

Meanwhile, the low pressure system will be absorbed into the main flow, driving a frontal passage through the area. BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: For the weekend, model disagreement continues. There are some signs in the ensemble data that temperatures could dip to near-average or even a tick below average for Saturday onward. This would be courtesy of a cold front moving in from the north.
BOU.text:
The above-average temperatures and mostly dry weather looks to roll on for the next few days for the vast majority of the forecast area. High temperatures should not approach record territory this week, though we expect high temperatures generally 5-10 degrees above average for the plains. Model guidance including ensemble clustering data remains in relatively good agreement through Friday on the evolution of the overall upper-level pattern.

A weak front has pushed through the area this evening, which will lead to high temperatures a touch cooler for Monday. There will be increased cloud cover overnight through Monday morning. The mountains could see some isolated rain/snow showers on Monday afternoon as moisture increases. The central mountains look to have the highest chances overall, though PoPs remain low. Little to no accumulation is expected. It will be rinse and repeat on Tuesday and Wednesday with some isolated rain/snow showers (at best) possible for the southern half of the high country. Temperatures should bump up a touch on both days as an upper-level ridge builds.

An upper-level low over the Pacific Ocean is expected to start to approach California on Wednesday, move inland, and be centered over Utah by Friday morning. The latest data shows a broadening trough moving into WY and MT on Friday afternoon. As this low approaches, flow aloft is expected to turn to the southwest for our area and stay southwest as the trough moves off to our northwest. Late Wednesday into Thursday, we expect deeper moisture to approach our southern and western high country. Precipitation chances should increase from south to north across the high country starting Wednesday evening and lasting through at least Friday morning with some low-impact snow possible (i.e. below advisory level) mainly above 11,500 ft or higher. PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: isolate precip Tues with somewhat drier Wednesday during the daylight hours, but shower will pick up Wednesday evening into Friday, especially over the central mtns, valleys and west slopes of the mtns adjacent to the plains.
PUB.text:
A deep trough is fcst to form over the western CONUS and then move slowly east through mid to late week. This trough will draw up tropical moisture into the SJU mtn. Given this...

Scattered showers are expected during the Tuesday time frame. Wednesday will likely see little if any precip SJU mtns, but the precip will ramp up Wednesday evening and last into Friday. The precip will likely be heavy as a review of the guidance shows a direct moisture tap coming into the sju mtns. Statistical products (NBM 1 viewer) are showing 2-3" of liquid with this first round of precip. Since this moisture source is coming directly into the region from the subtropics, it will be warm and most, if not all, of the precip will be rain.

A second round of lift will move over the SJU mtns from late Sunday through Monday. This forcing will be more associated with the mid level 500 mb trough, and temps will be colder. This will allow for the precip to have a bit more snow with it, and another inch or so of liquid equivalent will be possible.

As has been mentioned in several previous AFDs, The SJU mtn region is soaked and any additional heavy precip is likely going to cause high water issues. Additionally, looking at visible sat pix imagery, there appears to be quite a bit of fresh snow in place over the higher peaks of the SJU mtns, and the upcoming heavy rain combined with snow melt could make the high water issues worse. Folks who live in the region OR are traveling in this region are strongly urged to pay attention to later forecast regarding this upcoming weather situation. All the typical hazards associated with heavy rain in the mtns will be possible (rock slides/flash flooding)

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: The unsettled pattern will continue into the weekend as the closed low gradually translates to the east over the Desert Southwest, placing us in a region of weak zonal flow aloft.
CYS.text:
The long term period starts out mild and quiet as we remain on the western periphery of a longwave ridge, placing us in a southwesterly flow regime. As a result, high temperatures on both Wednesday and Thursday will peak 10-15 degrees above climatology (average high for Cheyenne on Thursday is 57F). The southwesterly flow will allow for a surge of mid to upper-level moisture from Baja California ahead of an amplified closed low located off the coast of California. Latest NAEFS guidance suggests PWAT near the climatological maximum on Thursday (~0.75"), which is quite remarkable given that our southwestern monsoon pattern typically ends in early to mid September. The main question will be if we can actually translate any of this rich moisture down to the surface as precipitation, which has been difficult to do so far this year. Unfortunately, our prospects aren't exactly looking favorable for any widespread QPF as the main synoptic-scale forcing for ascent is temporally offset from the primary moisture plume. The main DCVA combined with weak isentropic ascent looks to be over SE Wyoming sometime on Friday, which also looks like the day with our best chance for showers. Thunderstorm chances look to be low at this time as LREF guidance and forecast soundings show MLCAPE generally below 100 J/Kg, with slightly higher values in the Panhandle. Friday also looks to be quite mild, with median high temperatures per LREF guidance staying in the mid 60s to mid 70s east of the I-25 corridor, and primarily 50s west of the Laramie Range.

The unsettled pattern will continue into the weekend as the closed low gradually translates to the east over the Desert Southwest, placing us in a region of weak zonal flow aloft. Again, not overly enthusiastic about chances for widespread precipitation across SE Wyoming and the Nebraska Panhandle given that forcing for ascent is rather weak. SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: - The late week storm will also bring modest snowfall to the high terrain across northern Utah on Friday, with 3-6" possible mainly above 9000 feet.
SLC.text:
- Isolated showers and thunderstorms are possible each afternoon through Tuesday.

- Widespread precipitation returns late Wednesday across southern Utah, with coverage expanding northward through Friday. Many areas will see precipitation accumulations between 0.5-1.5" through this period, with locally up to 2.0-2.5".

- The late week storm will also bring modest snowfall to the high terrain across northern Utah on Friday, with 3-6" possible mainly above 9000 feet.

BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: Temperatures are forecast to be near normal Saturday through Sunday, with another significant upper-level trough looking to impact the area Sunday. Behind the earlier system, snow levels are lower at 6500 ft MSL.
BOI.text:
A sharp cooldown, precipitation, thunder, and winds are all in store as successive troughs of low pressure move through the area. Wednesday through Friday, a closed low off the coast of California will rejoin the broader flow as a trough amplifies over the Pacific Northwest. A slight ridge axis over the region will allow slight warming on Wednesday as clouds increase ahead of the approaching Californian low. Temperatures that afternoon will be 10-15 degrees above normal. Wednesday evening, precipitation chances begin to increase substantially to 50-70%. Broad cloud cover will inhibit instability, but the colder atmospheric mid-layer with still warm surface temperatures allow for a 10-20% chance of thunder Wednesday evening. Clouds, precipitation, and a colder airmass moving in drop temperatures to near normal on Thursday, with precipitation chances still 50-80% and just warm enough for a 10% chance of thunder that afternoon and evening. Before precipitation tapers off Friday evening, Friday morning the cold front passes, cooling temps to about 5 degrees below normal and bringing wind gusts up to 25-35 mph out of the NW. Winds remain strong through Friday evening. Over the course of the event, rainfall accumulation is forecast at 0.05-0.3 tenths in lower elevations, and 0.25-0.5 inches for mountain valleys. Mountain summits and ridges could see 0.5-1 inch of rainfall, and 1-4 inches of snow on summits above 8000 ft MSL. Snow is unlikely on mountains until Friday morning.

Temperatures are forecast to be near normal Saturday through Sunday, with another significant upper-level trough looking to impact the area Sunday. Behind the earlier system, snow levels are lower at 6500 ft MSL. Precipitation on Sunday will fall as snow in mountain passes and the highest mountain towns if the temperature forecast holds steady. Also behind the earlier trough, mountain valley cold pools could support fog/stratus formation and allow snowfall in the valleys on Sunday.
